Ballentine v. Hall, No. 1:26-cv-02331 — Rule 26(f) Conference and Proposed Judicial
Subject:
Counsel:
On October 16, 2026, I initiated the Rule 26(f) conference process in writing and requested responses by
October 30, 2026. As of today, October 28, I have received no response from NCMEC or Katie Hall.
Rule 26(f)(2) places responsibility for arranging and participating in the conference on the parties
collectively. I remain prepared to conduct the conference and develop the required discovery plan.
Prior correspondence raised the prospect of a motion to stay discovery upon initiation of the Rule 26(f)
process. No such motion has been filed, and no order staying the parties' Rule 26(f) obligations has been
entered.
I write to ascertain the respective positions of NCMEC and Katie Hall and determine whether judicial
intervention is necessary. Specifically:
1. Participation: Do NCMEC and Katie Hall intend to participate in the Rule 26(f) conference?
2. Basis for nonparticipation: Does either defendant contend that any existing order or other
authority excuses or postpones its Rule 26(f) obligations? If so, please identify that authority.
3. Proposed judicial relief: Would either defendant oppose an order directing the parties to
conduct the Rule 26(f) conference by a date certain and submit a discovery plan identifying any
unresolved disagreements? If so, on what grounds?
Please identify each defendant's position separately, including any differences between their respective
positions.
The October 30 response deadline established in my original correspondence remains unchanged. My
objective is to determine whether the parties can fulfill their obligations without requiring the Court's
intervention.
Marvelle J. Ballentine
Plaintiff, pro se

Re: Ballentine v. Hall, No. 1:26-cv-02331 — Rule 26(f) Conference and Proposed Judicial
Subject:
Mr. Ballentine, I believe a Rule 26(f) conference is premature at this juncture, as both Meta and my
clients have dispositive motions pending which-- if granted in full-- would be fully dispositive of all
claims. At a minimum, we do not yet know what claims (if any) will survive dismissal, or whether you
will seek leave to amend further in the event that the matter is dismissed, so without knowing what
claims are relevant, it seems premature to be planning discovery.
Thanks,
Padraic K. Keane
